narrative:
The model determined that you have a 95% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process heavily weighs this predicted outcome, your law school application was rejected.

The three factors that most strongly drove this decision were your LSAT score, your class ranking after the third year of law school, and your class ranking after the first year. In that order of importance, each of these pushed the prediction strongly toward failure rather than success.

Your LSAT score of 18 sits far below the average of 37 among students who were accepted, and this gap had the single largest negative impact on your chances. Your third-year ranking placed you in the bottom decile (1 out of 10), compared with an average around the middle of the class for accepted students; this was the second strongest factor pulling the prediction toward failure. Your first-year ranking was also at the very bottom decile, further reinforcing the same concern, though it carried slightly less weight than the later ranking.

Your low undergraduate GPA, low family income, and plan to attend full-time played only minor roles and did not meaningfully change the outcome.

To improve your prospects, focus first on raising your LSAT score through intensive preparation, then work to move your class rank upward in future years. These two areas offer the clearest path to shifting future predictions in your favor. (218 words)
